svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "The membrane is fluid: phospholipids move sideways within their layer all the time (lateral diffusion)."], [4, "Proteins float in the bilayer like a mosaic and can drift too, unless they are anchored to the cytoskeleton."], [8, "Cholesterol sits between the phospholipids and controls how fluid the membrane is. Phospholipids rarely flip from one layer to the other."]]
svg.title: Fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane
svg.desc: A section of plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails, cholesterol, channel and carrier proteins, a peripheral protein, a glycoprotein and a glycolipid. Inset: one phospholipid.
svg.text: Fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane
A section through the membrane, about 7–10 nm thick. Not to scale.

g.data-info: Watery: carbohydrate chains face this side only.
Non-polar, so they repel water and face each other in the middle of the bilayer: a barrier to ions and polar molecules.
Polar, so it is attracted to water: the heads face the watery fluid inside and outside the cell.
Between the phospholipids in animal cells: regulates fluidity (less fluid when warm, stops it becoming rigid when cold) and reduces permeability to ions.
Integral protein with a hydrophilic pore: lets specific ions or water (aquaporins) diffuse through. Some are gated.
Integral protein that changes shape to move a specific molecule across: facilitated diffusion, or active transport using ATP (pumps).
Protein with a carbohydrate chain on the outer surface: cell recognition, receptors (e.g. for hormones), and cell adhesion.
Phospholipid with a carbohydrate chain: cell recognition (e.g. ABO blood group antigens).
Attached to the surface (here the inner surface), not embedded: e.g. enzymes, or links to the cytoskeleton.
Two layers of phospholipids, tails inwards. About 7–10 nm thick.
A phosphate group and glycerol (hydrophilic head) joined to two fatty acids (hydrophobic tails). Amphipathic: one end attracts water, the other repels it.
